title: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') in Jirafeau
description: Jirafeau normally prevents browser preview for text files due to the possibility that for example SVG and HTML documents could be exploited for cross site scripting. This was done by storing the MIME type of a file and allowing only browser preview for MIME types beginning with image (except for image/svg+xml, see CVE-2022-30110, CVE-2024-12326 and CVE-2025-7066), video and audio. However, it was possible to bypass this check by sending a manipulated HTTP request with an invalid MIME type like image. When doing the preview, the browser tries to automatically detect the MIME type resulting in detecting SVG and possibly executing JavaScript code. To prevent this, MIME sniffing is disabled by sending the HTTP header X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
cwe: CWE-79 CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

title: @zereight/mcp-gitlab Vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery
description: `@zereight/mcp-gitlab` is a Model Context Protocol server for GitLab. Starting in version 0.0.1 and prior to version 2.1.27, when the environment variable `ENABLE_DYNAMIC_API_URL=true` is set, the server reads the `X-GitLab-API-URL` HTTP request header and uses it as the base URL for all outbound GitLab API calls made within that request. The server validates that the value is a well-formed URL (`new URL(dynamicApiUrl)`) but applies no allowlist or hostname restriction. The server then attaches the victim's `Private-Token` to every outbound fetch that uses the redirected URL. Any caller who can reach the HTTP transport can set `X-GitLab-API-URL` to an attacker-controlled host. The next GitLab API call the server makes delivers the victim's token to that host. Version 2.1.27 contains a patch.

title: @zereight/mcp-gitlab's unauthenticated arbitrary file read via `upload_markdown` enables PAT exfiltration and full account takeover
description: `@zereight/mcp-gitlab` is a Model Context Protocol server for GitLab. Prior to version 2.1.27, the SSE transport mode (`SSE=true`) exposes all MCP tools without any authentication. The `upload_markdown` tool reads arbitrary files from the server's local filesystem via an unsanitized `file_path` parameter and uploads them to a GitLab project. Combined, any unauthenticated network-reachable attacker can read `/proc/self/environ` to steal the server's `GITLAB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN` and achieve full GitLab account takeover. This is the default configuration for Docker deployments. Version 2.1.27 contains a patch.
cwe: CWE-22 CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

title: @zereight/mcp-gitlab: DNS rebinding reaches local Streamable HTTP MCP transport
description: `@zereight/mcp-gitlab` is a Model Context Protocol server for GitLab. Versions prior to 2.1.30 expose the Streamable HTTP MCP endpoint without an effective Host or Origin allowlist. A malicious web page can use DNS rebinding to route browser requests to a victim's local MCP listener while preserving an attacker-controlled `Host` and `Origin`. The server accepts those headers and reaches the MCP initialization path instead of rejecting the request at the HTTP boundary. Version 2.1.30 contains a patch.
cwe: CWE-350 CWE-350: Reliance on Reverse DNS Resolution for a Security-Critical Action

title: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ('Eval Injection') in hMailServer
description: Eval injection in the JScript event-script dispatcher in Progressive Robot Ltd's hMailServer, versions 6.0.0 through 6.3.3 on Windows, allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to run arbitrary JScript inside the hMailServer service process, with the privileges of the service account, via a password containing a backslash followed by an apostrophe, sent in any logon (SMTP AUTH, POP3, IMAP) that names an existing, active account. Exploitation requires a non-default configuration: event scripting enabled (off by default), the script language set to JScript (the default is VBScript), and an OnClientValidatePassword handler defined in the event script. The server wrote event values into the handler call as JScript string literals, escaping the apostrophe but not the backslash, so such a value closes the literal and the rest of it is parsed as script. The same flaw is reachable by a remote POP3 server through the message UID it returns, where an OnExternalAccountDownload handler is defined, and by a remote SMTP server through the error reply it rejects a delivery with, where an OnDeliveryFailed handler is defined. Before 6.2.25 the injected script can create any COM object, and from 6.2.25 it can with the default ScriptAllowedObjects value of '*'; WScript.Shell among them gives command execution as the service account. VBScript event scripts and the Linux builds of Progressive Robot Ltd's hMailServer are not affected.
cwe: CWE-95 CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code ('Eval Injection')
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.4. Until then, write the event handlers in VBScript, or define no OnClientValidatePassword, OnExternalAccountDownload or OnDeliveryFailed handler in JScript.

title: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in hMailServer
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the legacy Blowfish decryption routine (BlowFishEncryptor::DecryptFromString) in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.3 on Windows allows a local interactive user with no hMailServer credentials to write bytes of their choosing past the end of a 255-byte heap buffer in the hMailServer service process, which runs as LocalSystem by default. The user does this by passing a long hexadecimal string to the COM method Utilities.BlowfishDecrypt, which checked no authentication. The routine converted hexadecimal input of any length into a fixed 255-byte buffer before decrypting it in place. The result is a denial of service (service crash), and possibly code execution with the privileges of the service account.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which also requires authentication for the COM Utilities helpers (6.3.4 is the first release with this routine fixed).

title: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in hMailServer
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the legacy Blowfish encryption routine (BlowFishEncryptor::Encode, called by EncryptToString) in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allows an authenticated mailbox user to cause a denial of service (service crash), and possibly other unspecified impact. In 6.3.4 and 6.3.5, where the self-service REST API is enabled (it is off by default), the user does this remotely by adding a fetch account whose password is 129 to 247 characters long and not a multiple of 8, and then requesting their personal data export (GET /api/v1/me/export.zip), which encrypts that password with the legacy scheme. The same flaw is reachable on Windows by any local interactive user with no hMailServer credentials, through the COM method Utilities.BlowfishEncrypt, which checked no authentication. It is also reachable by every stored-secret write when ProtectStoredSecretsWithDPAPI is set to 0. For such a length, the routine's padding loop writes up to 7 zero bytes 2 to 232 bytes past the end of its 255-byte heap buffer. The ciphertext it returns is still correct.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6. Until then: keep the REST API off (RestApiPort 0, the default) or open it only to trusted users; keep ProtectStoredSecretsWithDPAPI on (the default); do not grant remote DCOM activation to the hMailServer AppID; and do not give untrusted people an interactive logon on the server.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own code review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

description: Cross-site scripting in the webmail of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.2 through 6.3.5 allows a remote attacker who can send a user an encrypted message to run script in the webmail's origin with that user's session. A click saved the file, but if the user opened the attachment in a new tab, a part declared as text/html was rendered as a document of the webmail's origin and its script could read the mailbox, send mail and change the account through the REST API. The webmail is served only when the REST API is enabled, which it is not by default.

title: Synchronous Access of Remote Resource without Timeout in hMailServer
description: Missing network timeouts in the Linux builds of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.0 through 6.3.5 allow a remote attacker to hold server threads indefinitely and so stop outbound mail delivery (denial of service). The server set its socket timeouts in the form Windows takes, which Linux refuses, and its HTTPS clients read without a deadline, so a peer that accepts a connection and then sends nothing held the waiting thread for as long as the connection stayed open. The MTA-STS policy fetch, enabled by default, is made during outbound delivery to mta-sts.<recipient domain>, so anyone who can make the server deliver mail to a domain they control - for example as the envelope sender of a message that bounces - can hold delivery threads until outbound delivery stops. The same flaw affects the DANE TLSA query, the OAuth2 token request, the ACME client, and the ManageSieve and metrics listeners, which a silent client stops from serving anyone else. Windows builds are not affected.
cwe: CWE-1088 CWE-1088: Synchronous Access of Remote Resource without Timeout
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, where every one of these requests and listeners has a deadline on Linux as on Windows. Until then, on Linux: set MtaStsEnabled to 0 if outbound delivery stalls, keep ManageSieve and the metrics listener off or reachable only from trusted networks, and restart the service to release held threads.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own static-analysis review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision in hMailServer
description: The Linux live-update apply helper (hmailserver-update) of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 runs as root on a request file written by the unprivileged hmailserver service account, and took from that request the program used to verify an AppImage update's signature and the systemd unit to stop before reading the service account's files. An attacker who already runs code as the hmailserver service account, for example through another flaw in the mail server, can therefore have arbitrary code executed as root, on any Linux installation where the live update's path unit is active - the default for the project's .deb and .rpm packages - and on AppImage installations run under that unit.
cwe: CWE-807 CWE-807: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose helper takes the unit and the AppImage only from its own root-owned command line, refuses an AppImage request where that names none, confirms that the server has stopped, and verifies, runs and installs only copies it made after the stop, readable by root alone until they have verified. Install 6.3.6 with the package manager (apt or dnf) rather than through the live update. An AppImage run under the path unit keeps the helper script copied to /usr/lib/hmailserver/ when its update units were installed, which the AppImage's own update does not replace: copy 6.3.6's script there and give it --image in a drop-in for hmailserver-update.service. Until then: systemctl disable --now hmailserver-update.path, which turns the apply off while the update check and download go on. Windows, builds with -DHM_LIVE_UPDATE=OFF and the container image are not affected.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Origin Validation Error in hMailServer
description: Missing Host header validation and missing throttling of failed administrator sign-ins in the REST API listener of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allow a remote attacker to brute-force the server administrator's password through the administrator's own browser by DNS rebinding. The listener, which is off by default and bound to the loopback when enabled, answered requests whatever their Host header named, and a failed sign-in with the administrator's password from the loopback was neither auto-banned nor delayed. A web page whose host name the attacker rebinds to 127.0.0.1, opened in a browser on the server, can therefore send authenticated requests to the listener, read the answers and try administrator passwords at full speed until one is accepted, giving the attacker full administrative control of the mail server.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose REST listener refuses an unexpected Host before any authentication and delays a wrong administrator password on every route. Until then: keep the REST API off (RestApiPort 0, the default) or reach it only through a reverse proxy that checks the Host header; give the administrator a long random password and enrol its second factor; do not browse the web from the server.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Missing Authorization in hMailServer
description: Missing authorization on COM objects in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 (Windows only) lets a local interactive user with no hMailServer credential read and write arbitrary files as the service account and queue mail as any sender. The service registers its COM classes with no DCOM access or launch permission and calls CoInitializeSecurity with no security descriptor, so any user logged on at the console or over Remote Desktop can activate the classes in the running service; a hMailServer.Message, its Attachments and Attachment, and a hMailServer.FetchAccount created this way carry a credential that never authenticated. Attachments.Add(path) and Attachment.SaveAs(path) performed no authorization check, and Message.Save/Copy and FetchAccount.AccountID/Save performed none either up to 6.3.3 and from 6.3.4 treated a holder with no credential as the server's own event-script host. Because the service does not impersonate the COM caller, Attachments.Add reads any file the service account can read and returns it, Attachment.SaveAs writes attacker-chosen bytes to any path it can write (on a LocalSystem installation, code execution as SYSTEM), Message.Save queues outbound mail from any address past the SMTP checks, and FetchAccount attaches a mail-fetch job to any mailbox. The objects an Application handed out behave the same once a later Authenticate on that Application fails.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose COM API refuses a message or fetch account that carries no credential outside the server's own event scripts, serves and writes a file on the server's disk through a message to the server administrator alone, and adds Application.CreateMessage() so a signed-in program composes mail that carries its credential. Until then: Do not allow untrusted users to log on interactively (console or Remote Desktop) to the server host. There is no configuration switch that closes this before 6.3.6; restricting the DCOM AppID's launch/access permission to exclude INTERACTIVE would also close it.

title: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information in hMailServer

title: Heap-based Buffer Overflow in Git
description:
Affected versions of Git have a heap buffer overflow in the three-way merge
code (xdiff), which an attacker can trigger through a repository they
control.

When Git merges a file, it first adds up the size of the merged
output, allocates a buffer of that size, and then writes the output into
it. That total was kept in a 32-bit signed integer. The
conflict-marker-size attribute, which can be set from a committed
.gitattributes file, accepts any positive integer, and the markers are
written several times for every conflict. A small file with a huge marker
size and many separate conflicts can therefore push the total past 4 GiB,
so the integer wraps to a small value and Git writes attacker-controlled
merge output past the end of a buffer that is too small. At minimum this
crashes Git, and because the overflow is large and its contents are largely
attacker-controlled, worse heap corruption is possible.

Any command that does a textual three-way merge can trigger it, such
as git-merge(1), git-rebase(1), git-cherry-pick(1), and
git-merge-tree(1). The latter is most likely a target for Git forges,
which might use git-merge-tree(1) on the server-side to check
mergeability. When the server reads attributes from trees in the
repository (for example through attr.tree or --attr-source), any
user who can push branches and request that they be merged (for
example by opening a pull or merge request) can trigger the overflow
without anyone else doing anything, and the data they push is small
because the oversized output only appears during the merge.

The problem has been patched by computing the size as size_t and
checking every addition for overflow, so Git stops with an error
instead of overflowing.

Servers that cannot upgrade right away can add

* conflict-marker-size=7

to each repository's info/attributes as a workaround, which overrides
any in-tree .gitattributes, or turn off server-side mergeability checks for
untrusted repositories.
credits: Thanks [taise](https://hackerone.com/taise) for reporting this vulnerability through HackerOne

title: Missing Authorization in hMailServer
description: Missing authorization in the Sieve editheader action (6.2.22 through 6.3.6) and in the mail-rule Set header value action (6.0.0 through 6.3.6) of Progressive Robot hMailServer allows an authenticated user to make the server send mail as any address, DKIM-signed where the address is at a domain the server signs for. A Sieve script's editheader (addheader/deleteheader) could add or delete any header field except Received and Return-Path, and the server applies a script's header edits before it queues a redirect, so the redirected copy is sent as the script left it. The server signs a message's first delivery pass as the domain named in its From header wherever it signs DKIM for that domain and the message carries no signature of it. A script could therefore delete and re-add From - another account's address, or anyone's at a hosted domain - and redirect, so the server sent the message in that name and, for a hosted domain, signed it with that domain's DKIM key, a forgery aligned to pass the domain's DMARC; or, where another sender's domain is one the server signs for, delete the DKIM-Signature that sender's message arrived with, alter a field, and redirect, so the server re-signed the altered message as that sender's domain. editheader placed no restriction on From, Sender, Resent-From, Resent-Sender or DKIM-Signature. The editheader action was introduced in 6.2.22. In the mail-rule engine, a domain's or an account's rule's Set header value action could likewise set From, Sender, Resent-From, Resent-Sender or DKIM-Signature ahead of a forward or a copy, whoever the rule belonged to, so that an account acting on its own rules over COM, a domain administrator, or an API key confined to a domain (over the REST API from 6.3.4) could have the server forward or copy a message in the name of any address, signed, where that address is at a domain the server hosts with DKIM signing enabled, with that domain's key.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.7, which refuses a Sieve script that adds or deletes From, Sender, Resent-From, Resent-Sender or DKIM-Signature when the script is stored, and does not make such an edit at delivery for a script stored earlier (logged), while leaving Reply-To and other fields editable; and which lets only a server rule's Set header value action, which only the server administrator saves, set those five fields, refusing an account's or a domain's rule that sets one when it is saved and not setting it at delivery for one stored before (logged). Until then, where accounts need not set Sieve scripts, close the script surfaces: keep ManageSieve off (ManageSieveServerPort=0, the default) or bound to the loopback, and turn the REST API off where the webmail's filter editor is not wanted (RestApiPort=0, the default); and review active Sieve scripts for an addheader or deleteheader of From, Sender, Resent-From, Resent-Sender or DKIM-Signature followed by a redirect, and account and domain rules for a Set header value of one of those fields. There is no per-extension setting that turns editheader off while Sieve is in use.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Use of Less Trusted Source in hMailServer
description: Use of a less trusted source in the DKIM signing of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.6 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to have mail they write signed with the DKIM key of a domain the server hosts, so that it passes DKIM and DMARC for that domain at other receivers. With DKIM signing enabled for a hosted domain, the server signed every message on its first delivery pass as the domain named in its From header, before local delivery, whatever the message's origin and without checking that its sender had authenticated. A sender anywhere could therefore send the server, as ordinary inbound mail, a message whose From is any address at such a domain, and the server signed it with that domain's key. Every copy the server then sent on to an address outside carried a valid signature aligned with the forged From, whatever the domain's DMARC policy: an account's forward, a mail rule's forward or copy, a Sieve redirect, an alias or distribution list with an outside member, the mirror copy, a managed-list or journal copy, or a message released from quarantine. A signed copy can also be re-sent to other recipients while the domain's key is unchanged. Exploitation needs DKIM signing to be enabled for the hosted domain (it is off until configured) and, for the forgery to leave the server, a forward, alias, list or rule that carries the domain's mail to an outside address. The signer likewise signed a message submitted over authenticated SMTP as whatever hosted domain its From header named, a header authenticated SMTP does not hold to the submitting account, so that an account of one hosted domain could have mail written in the name of another hosted domain signed with that domain's key; this mattered where the server holds signed-in senders to their own envelope addresses (SmtpAuthenticatedSenderCheck, off by default), as the signature was then the remaining way for such mail to pass the other domain's DMARC policy.
cwe: CWE-348 CWE-348: Use of Less Trusted Source
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.7. It records on each message, and on every copy of it, whether the message came from outside: an SMTP session that did not authenticate and was not a submission the server's IP ranges allow without authentication, a download from an external account, or an imported file. It signs a message as its From domain only when an authenticated user submitted it (as another domain the server hosts only when the account may send as the address its From names), the server made it, or an IP range let it in as one of the server's own domains, so mail from outside and its forwards keep only the signatures they arrived with, and a signed-in account's message from an address at another hosted domain that the account may not send as is sent unsigned as that domain. Until then, do one of the following: publish a DMARC policy of quarantine or reject for each hosted domain the server signs for and set the server's DMARC failure score (DMARCFailureScore) at or above the spam delete threshold (SpamDeleteThreshold), so that such a message is refused on arrival; refuse it in an OnAcceptMessage event script when the client has not authenticated and the From header names a domain the server signs for; remove the forwards, rule forwards, Sieve redirects, alias and list members and mirror addresses that carry mail to outside addresses; or disable DKIM signing for the hosted domains, which alone of these also covers a signed-in account's submission. Rotate the DKIM key of any domain whose key may have signed forged mail.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Missing Authorization in hMailServer
description: Missing authorization in the Sieve notify action (6.2.22 through 6.3.6) and in the mail-rule Reply action (6.0.0 through 6.3.6) of Progressive Robot hMailServer allows an authenticated user to send mail through the server as any address. A Sieve notify sends a notification message, and its :from tag names the sender; the server set the notification's From header to that :from as the script wrote it, without checking that the address belongs to the account - the check that the Sieve vacation action applies to its own :from, and that the server applies to the sender of mail queued over COM or sent from the webmail. An account that can store a Sieve script (over ManageSieve, the REST API's self-service filter, or the administration interface) could therefore have the server send a notification from any address, on this server or anywhere; and where the claimed address is at a domain the server hosts with DKIM signing enabled, the server signed the notification with that domain's DKIM key, because it signs by the From header's domain, producing forged mail aligned to pass the domain's DMARC policy. The notify action and this behaviour were introduced in 6.2.22. In the mail-rule engine, a rule's Reply was likewise sent from whatever address the action named, whoever the rule belonged to, so that an account acting on its own rules over COM, a domain administrator, or an API key confined to a domain (over the REST API from 6.3.4) could have a domain's or an account's rule reply from any address, signed, where that address is at a domain the server hosts with DKIM signing enabled, with that domain's key.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.7, which uses a Sieve notify :from only when it is an address that reaches the account (the account's own address or an active alias of it) - otherwise the notification goes from the account's own address, logged - and refuses a notify :from that is not an address when the script is stored, as the vacation action already does; and which sends a reply of an account's or a domain's mail rule only from an address the rule's owner may send as, refusing any other when the rule is saved and not sending a reply stored with one before (logged). Until then, where accounts need not set Sieve scripts, close the script surfaces: keep ManageSieve off (ManageSieveServerPort=0, the default) or bound to the loopback, and turn the REST API off where the webmail's filter editor is not wanted (RestApiPort=0, the default); and review active Sieve scripts for a notify whose :from is not the account's own address or an alias of it, and account and domain rules for a reply from an address the rule's owner may not send as. There is no per-extension setting that turns notify off while Sieve is in use.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition in hMailServer
description: Unchecked input for a loop condition in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.6 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to stop the server carrying mail. The server bounds the mail it generates in response to a message - a rule forward, reply or copy, an account forward, a Sieve redirect, vacation or notify, a bounce, an out-of-office reply - by a counter it carries in the message's X-hMailServer-LoopCount header, and makes no more once the counter reaches the configured rule loop limit (5 by default); that is what ends a forwarding or auto-reply cycle in a bounded number of hops. X-hMailServer-LoopCount is an ordinary header that is not stripped from mail arriving from outside, and the server read it with a signed conversion and no validation, so a count below zero passed every test against the limit: a sender who sets X-hMailServer-LoopCount to a negative value, or on the Linux builds to a value above the 32-bit signed range that the conversion wraps to a negative one, lifts the bound, and a message that enters a generated-mail cycle then loops up to about two thousand million times, each hop a queued message and a delivery, filling the queue and disk and stopping mail service. The Sieve notify action (from 6.2.22) consulted no limit at all, and its increment of the count could overflow a signed integer; and an account could reset the counter on its own mail through a Sieve editheader of the header (from 6.2.22) or a rule Set header value action (all versions) ahead of a forward or redirect.
cwe: CWE-606 CWE-606: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.7, which reads X-hMailServer-LoopCount in one validated place (a count only when it is digits and never above the limit; anything else is read as the limit so no generated mail is made from it), holds a Sieve notify to the same limit, and refuses an account Sieve script or rule that edits the counter, and writes a line break in a header value as spaces unless it folds the line, so that no value a generated message is built from writes a field of its own. Until then there is no setting that stops the header being read or that turns Sieve off: reduce forwarding and auto-reply arrangements that can feed one another, keep the Sieve script surfaces closed to accounts (ManageSieveServerPort=0, the default, and the REST API off where it is not needed, RestApiPort=0, the default), review active Sieve scripts and account rules for a notify of the account's own address and for an edit of X-hMailServer-LoopCount, and watch the queue for a message generated far past the loop limit.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Use of Out-of-range Pointer Offset in mutt
description: heap OOB write in convert_file_from_to() via a crafted Content-Type header allows attacker to OOB write when email is used as a template.

title: Incorrect Default Permissions in hMailServer
description: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.6 allow a local authenticated user to run code as the mail server's high-privileged accounts when the product is installed in a folder whose permissions are inherited from a writable parent, such as the root of a drive. The installer places the server's programs in the Bin folder of the program folder and gives neither the program folder nor Bin any permissions of their own, so they inherit the parent's. Under the default location, Program Files, ordinary users receive only read and execute and the configuration is not affected; but the installer accepts any path without warning, and a program folder at the root of an NTFS volume inherits write access for a broad group - Authenticated Users (Modify) on a Windows client, Users (create files and folders) on Windows Server. A local user without administrator rights can then alter or replace the service program, which runs as LocalSystem or as the service's virtual account, or the programs an administrator runs elevated from Bin during setup and maintenance, or place a library in Bin that those programs load in place of the system copy, gaining code execution with those privileges. The default Program Files installation is not affected.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.7. Its hMailServer.exe /ProtectFolders, which setup runs at the end of every server installation and upgrade, gives the program folder, Bin and ControlPanel SYSTEM and the Administrators full control and Users read and execute (where every user could read the folder), nothing inherited, and, where another account owned one of them, makes the Administrators its owner and takes away that folder's own entries that let others change it; setup also gives a program folder it creates those permissions before it copies anything into it, and hardens, before its files, the existing folder of an installation of the Control Panel alone. 6.3.7 does not yet create a new program folder with those permissions already in place, harden the folder before setup's own steps on an upgrade, a repair or a server installation into a folder that already existed, refuse a link or junction on the program folder's path (it is logged), or list the files in Bin and ControlPanel by owner. Before upgrading an affected installation, or until it is upgraded, follow from an elevated Command Prompt the steps in the hMailServer documentation, ServiceAccount.md, "Before upgrading an installation at a drive's root": first note who owns the program folder and what is directly in it (dir /q /a "<folder>") and everything in Bin, ControlPanel, Events, WebAdmin, DBScripts, Addons and Languages (dir /q /s /a); then, for the program folder, then Bin, then ControlPanel, make the Administrators its owner (icacls "<folder>" /setowner *S-1-5-32-544, the folder alone, without /T); take away every entry of the folder's own but SYSTEM's, the Administrators' and deny entries, one account a line (icacls "<folder>" /remove:g: the Users' and the service's by their SIDs, the service's only where the server is installed; the two application package groups by theirs, *S-1-15-2-1 and *S-1-15-2-2; anybody else's by the name icacls lists; and an entry icacls lists by a SID that names no account with the documentation's PowerShell line); replace what it inherits (icacls "<folder>" /inheritance:r /grant:r *S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F *S-1-5-32-545:(OI)(CI)RX); and on Bin and ControlPanel, where the server is installed, give the service account back its read and execute - each icacls line reporting "Successfully processed 1 files"; or move the installation under Program Files. Reinstall the programs into a new folder that only the administrators may change, not over the installation, where accounts that are not administrators could sign in while the installation was exposed, where another account made the program folder or could change it before the installation, where anybody but SYSTEM, the Administrators or TrustedInstaller owned the program folder, a file directly in it, or Bin, ControlPanel, Events, WebAdmin, DBScripts, Addons or Languages or anything in them, or where one of the three folders had an entry of its own that let another account change it, or one the steps could not take away: setup leaves in place every file it does not ship, and puts the event script, which the service runs, and the scripts in Addons only where none is there, so read the old event script before copying it. Setup run into a folder without a settings file sets up a new, empty server there, so the settings file and the data go into the new folder first (ServiceAccount.md, "Reinstalling into a new folder"): stop the service and run nothing from the old folder, its uninstaller included; copy, not move, the mail, the built-in database's folder and the settings file into the new folder, the copies kept private; read the copy of the settings file, deleting its AdministratorPassword and each [Directories] line with a path in the old folder; then, with a 32-bit installation's uninstall entry taken away, run the release's setup with the new folder; read in the new Control Panel the programs the database's settings name, make the REST API's keys again, change each path the database holds into the old folder, and, once nothing names it, delete the old folder by hand.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient complexity in the Sieve filter evaluation of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.24 through 6.3.5 allows an authenticated account holder to make the mail services unavailable with their own filter. A ':matches' pattern was matched by a backtracking descent whose time grew with the matched value's length raised to the number of wildcards, so a pattern such as '*a*a*a*b' over 800 characters took 44 seconds; and 'deleteheader' erased the fields it removed one at a time, so removing many fields of one name over a message's header cost O(N^2) (80,000 fields took 18.8 seconds). Sieve filters run on the small, shared delivery thread pool, so an account holder whose active script does this, fed a few messages they can send themselves, empties the pool and stops delivery for the whole server. The script is the account holder's own and cannot be set for another user.
cwe: CWE-1333 CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which matches a ':matches' pattern by placing each piece once (time linear in the value times the pattern) and removes 'deleteheader' fields in one pass. Until then, review active Sieve scripts for ':matches' patterns with several wildcards and for 'deleteheader', and lower the maximum message size.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Incorrect Default Permissions in hMailServer
description: Incorrect default permissions in the Windows installer of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allow a local authenticated user to read the mail server's data. The installer created the data, log, temp, database and event folders and the hMailServer.INI configuration file with the permissions inherited from the installation folder, by default under Program Files, which give the local Users group read access. Any user who can sign in to the computer could read every stored message, the logs, the built-in database with the accounts' password hashes whenever the service is stopped, and the configuration file, including the database password, which is sealed only with the machine's DPAPI key and can be unsealed by any local account; with an external database that password gives full control of it. The Linux AppImage of 6.3.0 through 6.3.5 likewise created its per-user data folders readable by other local users.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose installer makes the data, log, temp, database and event folders and hMailServer.INI private to SYSTEM, the Administrators and the service at every installation and upgrade; then change the database password and the administrator password if accounts that are not administrators could sign in to the server. Until then, from an elevated prompt, remove the inherited entries for Users and the application package groups from those folders and the file with icacls (/inheritance:d, then /remove:g).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the JSON reader of Progressive Robot hMailServer allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the mail services unavailable. Reading a JSON object kept the first of each duplicated member name by searching the members already read, so an object of N distinct member names cost O(N^2): 1 MB took 8.9 seconds and 4 MB took 300 seconds against the affected code. A remote attacker reaches the reader without an account by mailing a crafted TLS-RPT report (up to 16 MB after decompression) to a hosted domain's published report mailbox, which is read on a delivery thread; a few such reports hold every delivery thread (ten by default), so the server delivers no mail, local or outbound, for over an hour per report. A signed-in account reaches the same 16 MB body through the webmail's own REST routes, holding the REST API's own worker threads. Where no report mailbox is configured, the unauthenticated REST sign-in routes that read a JSON body are capped at 64 KB and are not affected.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which keeps the member names seen in a hash set, so a JSON object is read in one pass. Until then, where domain reports are on, move the report mailbox off a hosted domain; restart the service to end a busy thread.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the SPF macro expansion of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to consume worker-thread time by publishing a crafted SPF record. RFC 7208 section 7.1 requires a name too long to look up to lose whole labels from the left; the server did this by removing one label at a time and copying the rest of the name each time, so the work grew with the square of the expansion. An attacker who publishes an SPF record for a domain they control, with a mechanism whose domain-spec expands through macros to a name far longer than 253 characters, makes the SPF check of a message from that domain take several seconds. The expansion is bounded by SPF's own per-term and per-macro limits, so the loss of availability is partial.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which finds where the name becomes short enough and cuts it once. Until then, turn SPF checking off, or accept the bounded delay.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the inbound DKIM and ARC signature verification of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the mail services unavailable by sending a message. Building the canonical header and choosing the header fields named in a signature's h= tag took time growing with the square of the message's header: the 'simple' canonicalisation prepended each continuation line of a folded field to the lines already gathered, and both canonicalisations searched the gathered fields from the bottom for each h= name and erased the match from the middle of the list. A message whose header holds very many fields, or a field folded over very many lines, with a DKIM-Signature the attacker signs for a domain they control, keeps a worker thread busy for tens of seconds per signature; up to ten signatures are evaluated per message by each of the DKIM and DMARC tests, on the threads that serve delivery and SMTP.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which builds the canonical header in one pass and chooses the h= fields from an index by name. Until then, lower the maximum message size, which bounds the cost.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop') in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity and a non-terminating loop in the MIME processing of received messages in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the mail services unavailable by sending a message. Removing a MIME header parameter whose value is empty and directly followed by a semicolon (for example a Content-Disposition with 'filename=a.bat; filename=;') entered a loop that never terminates, holding a worker thread at full load until the server is restarted; this is reached when the attachment blocker renames a blocked attachment or a filename is set over the REST API. Separately, decoding a header field that holds many RFC 2047 encoded words of an encoding other than base64 or quoted-printable, removing a parameter with many RFC 2231 continuations, and deleting many header fields of one name each took time growing with the square of the message, on the small thread pools that serve IMAP, SMTP and POP3 connections, delivery and the REST API.
cwe: CWE-835 CWE-835: Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop')
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which removes a MIME parameter and deletes header fields in a single pass and searches an encoded word's terminator only for a decodable word. Until then: lower the maximum message size (which bounds the quadratic paths but not the non-terminating one), and restart the service to end a hung thread.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following') in hMailServer
description: Improper link resolution and external control of file paths in the administrative command-line operations of hMailServer.exe in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 allow a local attacker who already runs code as the low-privilege service account to escalate privilege. On Windows, operations run with administrator rights by the installer, DBSetup, the Control Panel or an administrator wrote log entries and crash records into the log folder, created, deleted and changed the permissions of the self-signed certificate and private key in the data folder, and rewrote message files in the data folder, all by path in folders the service account (NT SERVICE\hMailServer, the default for new installations since 6.3.4) can modify, following junctions and mount points; and the store-maintenance operations reached files by names taken from the database, which the service account can write, including names outside the data folder. On Linux, the store-maintenance and object-storage operations run as root followed symbolic links the service account (the packaged hmailserver user, which owns the data folder) planted in it, so a root-run operation read, wrote or removed the link's target as root. A local attacker controlling the service account can thereby gain the administrator's (Windows) or root's (Linux) privileges when such an operation is run.
cwe: CWE-59 CWE-59: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, in which every administrative command writes nothing to the logs and arms no crash recorder, writes the certificate only through folders held open and checked from the drive's root, reaches no file a database row names outside the data folder, and walks the data folder before any store command - going through a junction or mount point only when the administrators alone own and control it and refusing any other; and on Linux a store or object-storage command run as root first drops to the service account, so it follows no link that account planted. Until then: on Windows run the service as LocalSystem, or stop the service and check the program folder's Logs, Data, Temp and Database folders for junctions, mount points and symbolic links and that no message row names a path outside the data folder; on Linux run the store commands only as the service user, never as root.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the bounce and complaint processing of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to stop mail delivery by sending messages, when bounce processing or complaint processing is enabled or a mailing list is managed by the server (none is by default). The readers of incoming delivery status notifications (RFC 3464) and abuse feedback reports (RFC 5965) removed the blank lines at the start of the returned headers part two bytes at a time, copying the rest of the part each time, so their work grew with the square of the number of blank lines. A message shaped like such a report, whose headers part begins with a very large number of blank lines within the reader's 2 MB limit, keeps a delivery thread busy for over a minute while it is delivered, and a few such messages a minute keep every delivery thread busy.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose report readers cut the leading blank lines off once. Until then, turn bounce processing, complaint processing and list management off (the default).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the decoding of message header fields in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the IMAP, SMTP and POP3 services, or the webmail, unavailable by sending a message. The server unfolded a decoded header value by finding each line break from the end of the value and removing it, moving the rest of the value each time, so its work grew with the square of the number of line breaks, and an RFC 2047 encoded word may decode to any number of them. A received message whose Subject or other header field holds such a value keeps a worker thread busy for minutes or longer each time the value is read: when the recipient's IMAP client searches, sorts or threads the folder by a header, when the webmail lists the folder, and, where configured, when a rule tests a header, a spam tag is added to the Subject or an abuse report is read during delivery. The IMAP worker threads are shared with SMTP and POP3, so a few such messages stop those services responding. The server's reading of a message header from its file also searched everything read so far after each 4,000 bytes, costing seconds for a header of tens of megabytes.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which unfolds a header value in one pass and searches a header being read only in what each read adds. Until then: lower the maximum message size, which bounds the cost (it grows with the square of the value's size); remove such a message over POP3; or keep the REST listener off (RestApiPort 0, the default).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 processes several IMAP commands from a signed-in account in time quadratic in the command's length or in the number of elements it names, and can be made to hold memory out of proportion to a command. The FETCH data-item parser normalised a BODY[] section with a case-insensitive string replacement that copied the whole item per occurrence and split the item list by repeatedly copying the remainder of the command; the server's case-insensitive search compared a needle afresh at every position, so a long SEARCH TEXT key over a message cost the product of the two lengths; SEARCH message sets and the saved-result marker ($), SORT criteria, HEADER.FIELDS name lists and UID ranges were each read once per message rather than once per command; and a FETCH naming a message's sections very many times read and held every section in memory before sending any. An IMAP command may continue past one line through non-synchronizing literals, so one command can reach about eleven megabytes. The IMAP worker threads are a small pool shared with SMTP and POP3, so a signed-in user sending such commands can make the IMAP, SMTP and POP3 services stop responding (CWE-407) and can consume excessive memory (CWE-400).
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which parses the FETCH command and runs the server's case-insensitive string operations in a single pass, reads each SEARCH and UID set and HEADER.FIELDS list once per command, substitutes the saved-result marker once, and refuses a FETCH whose sections add up to many times the message before sending any. There is no configuration workaround; the commands require only a signed-in account. Restricting IMAP access to trusted accounts and networks reduces who can send them.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the REST API (6.3.3 through 6.3.5) and the IMAP PREVIEW response (6.2.22 through 6.3.5) of Progressive Robot hMailServer allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the webmail, the administration console and the REST API unavailable by sending a message. To show a snippet of each message in a folder's message list, the server decoded the character entity references of a message that has an HTML part and no text part with a string replacement whose work grew with the square of their number. A received HTML-only message holding a very large number of entity references therefore keeps one of the listener's four worker threads busy for minutes or longer each time the recipient's webmail lists the folder, without the message being opened, so that a few such listings leave the HTTP listener unable to answer anybody. The IMAP PREVIEW response read such text the same way, holding an IMAP thread for each client that asks for the preview of such a message. The flaw is in the server's shared string class, whose replace and remove both ran in quadratic time.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose string replacement and removal write their result in one pass. Until then: lower the maximum message size, which bounds the cost (it grows with the square of the HTML's size); remove such a message over IMAP or POP3; or keep the REST listener off (RestApiPort 0, the default).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity in hMailServer
description: Inefficient algorithmic complexity in the webmail's message view of the REST API in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.2 through 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make the webmail, the administration console and the REST API unavailable by sending a message. The route that renders a received message's HTML replaced each reference to an embedded image in place, with work that grew with the square of the number of references, and wrote the image out for every reference while counting it against its size limit only once. A message whose HTML refers to one small embedded image a very large number of times, opened in the webmail by its recipient, therefore keeps one of the listener's four worker threads busy for minutes and makes it build a document of gigabytes, so that a few such messages leave the HTTP listener unable to answer anybody.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, in which the route reads a message's HTML once to find the images it names and once to write them, and writes at most 24 MB of inlined images in all, every reference counted. Until then: lower the maximum message size, which bounds the cost (it grows with the square of the HTML's size); leave the webmail's offline store off so that only an opened message triggers it; or keep the REST listener off (RestApiPort 0, the default).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Not Failing Securely ('Failing Open') in hMailServer
description: Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.0.0 through 6.3.5 fails open when applying DANE (RFC 7672) to outbound SMTP delivery. The server's validating DNSSEC resolver treated a TLSA or MX lookup that did not complete (no answer, SERVFAIL, a malformed reply), an answer without the requested records and without an NSEC/NSEC3 proof of their absence, and an answer whose records carried no applicable RRSIG as if the recipient domain were unsigned, and from 6.2.19 it also delivered to mail exchangers taken from an unvalidated MX lookup that the DNSSEC-validated MX record set did not name. An attacker who can drop, forge or strip DNS answers on the path to the server's resolver, at the resolver, or between the resolver and the recipient domain's name servers, and who holds an active position on the SMTP path, can thereby disable DANE for a DNSSEC-signed recipient domain and cause messages to be delivered in cleartext or to a host of the attacker's choosing with an arbitrary certificate, where they can be read and modified.
cwe: CWE-636 CWE-636: Not Failing Securely ('Failing Open')
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, which treats an incomplete, unsigned or unproven DNSSEC answer for a TLSA or MX lookup under a signed zone as indeterminate, does not use a mail exchanger whose lookup was indeterminate, defers the delivery when none is left, delivers only to mail exchangers named by a DNSSEC-validated MX record set, and (for a host whose DNS servers are IPv6 only) asks those IPv6 servers. Until then, for each recipient domain whose mail must be protected, an SMTP route that names its mail exchangers with the connection security 'STARTTLS (required)', with remote certificate verification on (VerifyRemoteSslCertificate=1), prevents delivery in cleartext or to another host for that domain; and the server's DNS resolver should be one reached over a trusted path, such as a validating resolver on the same host.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling in hMailServer
description: Uncontrolled eviction in the pending sign-in tables of the REST API in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.4 and 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to make other users' OpenID Connect, SAML and passkey sign-ins fail. The routes that start a single sign-on and hand out a passkey sign-in challenge are reached without authentication and stored pending state in bounded tables that dropped their oldest entry when full, whoever had started it. An attacker who starts sign-ins a few times a second (about a hundred a second for passkeys) pushes every other user's pending sign-in out of the table before that user's browser returns, denying single sign-on and passkey sign-in for as long as the requests continue.
cwe: CWE-770 CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, in which a pending OpenID Connect, SAML or passkey sign-in is no longer held on the server at all but carried by the browser in a cookie sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key held only in memory and good once, so there is no table a flood of unauthenticated starts can fill. Until then: limit the rate of /portal/oidc/start, /portal/saml/start and /api/v1/passkeys/challenge per client at a reverse proxy, and keep password sign-in available for administrators.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling in hMailServer
description: Uncontrolled eviction in the browser session table of the REST API in Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.2.28 through 6.3.5 allows a remote authenticated user to end other users' sessions. The table of browser sessions, shared by every account, the server administrator and support sessions, dropped its least recently used session whenever it was full, whoever it belonged to, and placed no limit on how many sessions one account could hold. A user who repeatedly signs in with their own mailbox password can therefore keep the table full and sign out every webmail and administration session that is idle for more than a short time, for as long as they continue.
cwe: CWE-770 CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, in which each account or administrator holds at most fifty sessions and gives up its own least recently used one, and a full table makes room out of the sessions of whoever holds the most. Until then: limit the rate of POST /api/v1/session per client at a reverse proxy in front of the listener, and disable an account found signing in repeatedly (its sign-ins are in the application log and its device list).
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Improper Certificate Validation in hMailServer
description: Improper certificate validation in the webmail of Progressive Robot hMailServer 6.3.2 through 6.3.5 allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to have S/MIME-encrypted mail that the account later sends to another correspondent also encrypted to the attacker's key. When its recipient opened a signed message, the webmail kept the signer's certificate for encrypting replies whether or not the server found its chain trusted, under the first e-mail address the certificate listed rather than the message's From address, and beside any certificate already held for that address. Encrypted mail later sent from the webmail to that address was encrypted to every certificate held for it, so a holder of the kept certificate's key who obtains a copy of such a message can read it.
solutions: Upgrade to hMailServer 6.3.6, whose webmail keeps a signer's certificate only when its chain is trusted, only under the From address the signature was verified for, and a different certificate for an address that has one only when the reader chooses to. After upgrading, review the correspondents' certificates on the webmail's Security page and remove any that should not be there. Until then: check the certificates listed for an address before sending it encrypted mail from the webmail, or encrypt in a mail program.
credits: Found in the hMailServer project's own security review (Progressive Robot Ltd)

title: Authentication Bypass by Spoofing in Jacamar CI
description: Insufficient job validation for service accounts in Jacamar CI prior to v0.30.0 allows authenticated CI users to generate arbitrary account names.

This issue presents a serious risk to all versions of Jacamar CI prior to v0.30.0

RunAs validation script to check for bot accounts. Please see the release notes for
a complete example.
